section_title: What does God’s saving desire tell us about prayer?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 3 This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, 4 who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

context_lines: These verses give a reason for the instruction just before them: prayer for everyone, including kings and those in authority. Paul calls that prayer good and pleasing in God our Savior’s sight.

He describes God as wanting everyone to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. The following verses connect that concern with the one mediator, Christ Jesus, His self-giving and Paul’s mission to the Gentiles.

The statement belongs to an appeal for broad prayer and the proclamation of Christ. It is not presented here as a guarantee that every person will finally be saved, nor as a reason to exclude particular groups from prayer.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians agree that prayer should reach beyond our own circle, including rulers and people unlike us. They differ in how they understand everyone in the statement about God’s saving desire.

[Calvin’s comments on verses 3–4](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/1_timothy/2.htm) read the passage as including every rank and nation, especially rulers and Gentiles. He understands the emphasis as all kinds of people, rather than a statement about God’s purpose for every individual. This is a named Reformed reading, not a claim that every Reformed teacher phrases the distinction identically.

[Wesley’s notes on verses 3–6](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-timothy/) read God’s saving desire as extending to every person, while distinguishing that desire from compulsion. The Catholic [Catechism, paragraph 851](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_two/chapter_three/article_9/paragraph_3_the_church_is_one,_holy,_catholic,_and_apostolic.html), also expressly describes God as willing everyone’s salvation through the knowledge of the truth. These readings give a wider individual scope to the desire described here.
The difference does not remove the practical instruction to pray broadly. Paul places that instruction beside the one God, Christ’s mediation and His self-giving for others.
god_plan_lines: [Jeremiah 29:4–7](https://biblehub.com/bsb/jeremiah/29.htm) provides an earlier parallel: God tells the exiles to seek Babylon’s welfare and pray for the city where they live. Prayer for the wider society already belongs within the faithful life of God’s people amid people who do not share their faith.

[Ephesians 3:5–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/3.htm) describes Gentiles sharing the promise and the same body through the gospel. Paul’s mission to the Gentiles, named in verse 7, serves that wider purpose. Prayer crosses the boundaries of rank and nation because the message of Christ is to reach beyond them.
current_position_lines: In [Prayer and Faith](https://thewayofscripture.com/studies/prayer-and-faith.html), we identify God’s stated desire for everyone to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth as part of His revealed will. That gives our prayer a clear direction: seek people’s salvation and their knowledge of Him, in keeping with what He has made known.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Prayer and Faith, What His Will Actually Means, lines 25–44: 1 Timothy 2:3–4 as God’s revealed saving desire and knowledge of truth, guiding prayer. No new ruling on election or the extent of atonement.
